strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-studied question: whether pretraining hyperparameters optimized for validation loss also optimize downstream (post-fine-tuning) performance, bridging pretraining and post-training literatures.

Extensive experimental design spanning two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (up to 4B), two training regimes (20 TPP and 140 TPP compute-optimal/overtrained), six diverse fine-tuning tasks, and six evaluation metrics covering both correctness and quality.

The paper is appropriately cautious about the strength of its correlational claims; e.g., it explicitly runs a leave-one-out stability analysis (Fig. 3/9) showing that the pretraining-loss-vs-downstream-performance correlation is unstable, rather than overselling a fragile correlation.

The mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix pseudo-rank, train-val gap for overfitting) provides a multi-pronged, theoretically grounded (e.g., connecting to Kobayashi et al. 2024's nuclear-norm argument, Jacot et al. 2024's neural collapse) attempt to explain the observed plasticity effect, going beyond a purely empirical correlation.
Thorough appendix documentation of hyperparameters, datasets, and additional per-task/per-metric results, aiding reproducibility.

The core empirical finding (higher-than-default weight decay improves downstream fine-tuning performance) is reasonably consistent across the many settings tested, which is a nontrivial and potentially impactful result for pretraining practice.
weaknesses: Weight decay sweeps are very sparse for the larger/more expensive configurations: Llama-2-4B-20x is tested at only two values (0.1 and 1.0), and OLMo-2-1B-140x at only three values (0.1, 0.3, 1.0). Claims about the 'optimal' weight decay for these settings are therefore weakly supported—the reported optimum may simply be the better of very few options tested, not a true optimum.

No mention of multiple seeds or repeated fine-tuning/pretraining runs; given that several test sets are small (e.g., PubMedQA n=1000, MMLUProCoT n=567) and some reported downstream accuracy differences are modest, the absence of variance estimates or significance testing makes it hard to assess how much of the observed trend is signal versus noise.

The three proposed mechanisms (linear separability, attention rank reduction, reduced train-val overfitting gap) are established as being correlated with weight decay and, in one case, correlated with downstream performance (Fig. 15), but no causal or interventional evidence (e.g., directly manipulating rank or separability independent of weight decay) is provided to confirm these are actually the drivers of plasticity rather than co-occurring epiphenomena.

Model scale is modest (up to 4B parameters, trained on relatively small token budgets); it remains unclear whether the findings generalize to the much larger models and dataset scales used in modern frontier LLM pretraining, which the paper's motivation section explicitly targets.

The range of weight decay values differs inconsistently across model setups (e.g., Llama models tested up to 10.0, OLMo models only up to 1.0), which complicates direct cross-family comparisons and obscures whether the identified 'optimal' values are truly comparable across settings.

Fine-tuning hyperparameters (e.g., whether weight decay is also used during SFT, and its value) are not clearly discussed, leaving open a potential confound between pretraining weight decay effects and fine-tuning regularization.

For the 140 TPP regime, the paper notes the optimal weight decay for downstream performance (0.3) is lower than for 20 TPP (1.0) but higher than the pretraining-loss-optimal value (0.1), yet the very sparse grid (3 points) prevents confident characterization of this trend, and extrapolation to longer training in the discussion is speculative.

strengths: Addresses a timely and under-explored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters chosen to minimize validation loss are optimal for downstream (post-fine-tuning) performance. This end-to-end framing is a useful departure from the usual loss-only view of scaling/hyperparameter studies.

Reasonably broad experimental matrix: two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (0.5B-4B), two TPP regimes (20x, 140x), six fine-tuning tasks, and six evaluation metrics, which gives some breadth to the central claim that higher weight decay improves downstream accuracy.

The paper attempts a multi-pronged mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix pseudo-rank, train-val loss gap) that at least tells a coherent, if speculative, story connecting weight decay to plasticity.

Commendable transparency: the authors explicitly show that the Pearson correlation between pretraining loss and downstream performance is unstable under leave-one-out removal (Figure 9) rather than hiding this weakness, which is an honest treatment of a limitation that undercuts their own correlation claims.
The practical implication (default weight decay of 0.1 may not be optimal when downstream adaptability is the goal) is a concrete, actionable claim relevant to practitioners.
weaknesses: Weight decay sweeps are very uneven and often extremely sparse for the larger/more expensive models: Llama-2-4B-20x has only two values (0.1 and 1.0), and OLMo-2-1B-140x has only three (0.1, 0.3, 1.0). Conclusions about 'optimal' weight decay and trends across TPP regimes rest on 2-3 point curves for exactly the settings (larger models, overtrained regime) that matter most for real-world pretraining decisions.

No repeated seeds or error bars are reported anywhere in the main results (pretraining loss curves, downstream accuracy curves, probing accuracy, rank curves, train-val gap). Given that downstream accuracy differences between weight decay settings are sometimes small relative to visible non-monotonicities in the plots (e.g., Figure 2's dips and bumps), it is impossible to assess whether the reported trends are statistically meaningful or within run-to-run noise.

The paper's own stability analysis (Figure 3, Figure 9) shows that the correlation between pretraining loss and downstream performance changes sign and magnitude under leave-one-out removal, which is used to support 'Finding 2,' but this same instability should also cast doubt on the robustness of the main weight-decay-improves-downstream claim, since both are derived from the same small, noisy set of data points per model.

The mechanistic explanations in Section 5 (linear separability, attention rank, overfitting) are purely correlational/observational; no causal intervention (e.g., directly manipulating representation separability or attention rank independent of weight decay) is performed to establish that these mechanisms actually mediate the plasticity effect. The language throughout ('potential explanation', 'may prevent', 'conjecture') signals that these are post-hoc narratives rather than validated mechanisms.

Fine-tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs) are held fixed across all pretrained checkpoints regardless of weight decay, which could confound the comparison — a base model pretrained with very different weight decay may require a different fine-tuning learning rate to adapt optimally, so observed 'plasticity' differences could partly reflect fine-tuning hyperparameter mismatch rather than an intrinsic property of the base model.

Appendix Figure 7 reveals substantial heterogeneity across the six downstream tasks, with some tasks (e.g., SimpleScaling, with very low absolute accuracy near 0.01-0.03) showing noisy, non-monotonic, or negligible effects of weight decay, which is not adequately discussed in the main text; the averaged metrics in Figure 2 could be masking this heterogeneity and overstating the generality of the effect.

The downstream-task evaluation set, while six tasks, is dominated by relatively narrow CoT/QA formats and all fine-tuning is single-stage SFT; it is unclear how well the plasticity findings would generalize to RLHF/RL-style post-training or to safety/alignment tuning, which the paper itself flags as future work rather than addressing.

The overall sample size of independently pretrained models is small (especially for 4B and 140 TPP settings), and because pretraining runs are expensive single-run experiments, the paper cannot rule out that observed 'optimal' weight decay values are specific artifacts of a single training run rather than a reproducible property of the weight decay hyperparameter.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters optimized for validation loss are also optimal for downstream (post-trained) performance. This reframes HP selection in a way that is directly relevant to how LLMs are actually developed in two stages.

Experimental breadth is a major strength: two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (0.5B-4B), two training regimes (20 TPP compute-optimal and 140 TPP overtrained), six diverse fine-tuning tasks, and six evaluation metrics capturing both correctness and solution quality. The consistency of the core finding (higher-than-default weight decay improves downstream performance) across this breadth of settings is persuasive.

The paper goes beyond a purely correlational headline finding and attempts three complementary mechanistic analyses (linear probing of representations, attention matrix rank via pseudo-rank, and train-val loss gap as an overfitting proxy), each tied to plausible theoretical motivations from prior literature (neural collapse, low-rank attention from weight decay, stability-plasticity tradeoff). This triangulation strengthens the plausibility of the causal story even if each piece alone is not conclusive.

The authors are appropriately cautious in some places, e.g., explicitly reporting that the pretraining-loss-vs-downstream-performance correlation is unstable under leave-one-out resampling (Figure 9) rather than overstating this relationship, and noting that extrapolation beyond 140 TPP is untested.
Good reproducibility support: detailed appendices specify architectures, training/fine-tuning hyperparameters, dataset sizes, and weight decay sweep values for every model configuration.

The finding that the pretraining-loss-optimal weight decay and the downstream-optimal weight decay diverge, and can even trade off (higher WD worse pretraining loss, better downstream performance) in the overtrained regime, is a concrete, falsifiable, and interesting empirical result with practical implications for hyperparameter tuning pipelines.
weaknesses: Scale is modest relative to modern frontier pretraining (up to 4B parameters, up to 140 TPP), and the paper's own discussion acknowledges uncertainty about whether findings extrapolate to much larger models or much longer training runs; the practical relevance to current large-scale LLM development is therefore somewhat speculative.

No evidence of multiple seeds or repeated pretraining/fine-tuning runs is reported; each weight decay value appears to correspond to a single pretraining run and a single fine-tuning run per task. Given documented instability of correlation estimates (Figure 9) and noisy few-shot/sampling-based metrics (Maj@16, RM@16, etc.), the lack of variance estimates or error bars makes it hard to assess whether reported differences in downstream accuracy reflect a genuine weight-decay effect versus run-to-run noise.

Fine-tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, batch size) are held fixed across all pretrained checkpoints rather than tuned per weight-decay setting. Since plasticity/trainability can interact with optimal fine-tuning LR, it is unclear whether the observed advantage of higher pretraining weight decay is a general property or an artifact of this fixed downstream optimization recipe; a brief per-checkpoint fine-tuning LR sweep (even on one task) would substantially strengthen the causal claim.

The operationalization of 'plasticity' is essentially identical to 'downstream fine-tuning accuracy,' which conflates plasticity (ability to update/learn new information) with other factors such as pretrained knowledge, representation quality, or alignment with the fine-tuning distribution. The paper would benefit from more directly isolating plasticity (e.g., using canonical plasticity diagnostics such as learning speed curves within fine-tuning, loss-of-plasticity style sequential adaptation tasks) rather than inferring plasticity solely from final fine-tuned performance.

The mechanistic experiments are not uniformly applied across all five model/training setups (e.g., the overfitting/train-val-gap analysis in Figure 6 is shown only for OLMo-2-1B at 20 TPP, and some attention-rank results differ notably between Llama-2 and OLMo-2, e.g., Figure 16 vs Figure 5), which limits confidence that the proposed mechanisms generalize as broadly as the main plasticity finding itself.

Pretraining data and setup diversity is limited to two corpora (FineWeb-Edu, OLMo-Mix-1124); it remains unclear whether the weight-decay-plasticity relationship is sensitive to data quality/composition, which is a major axis of variation in real pretraining pipelines.

The weight decay values identified as optimal (up to 1.0, 10x the common default) are unusually large and outside typical practitioner ranges; the paper does not fully explore why such extreme values would be adopted in practice given their cost to pretraining loss, nor does it offer a principled method (e.g., a scaling law) for choosing weight decay for downstream objectives, limiting the actionable takeaway beyond qualitative guidance.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic empirical study spanning two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple scales (0.5B-4B), two training regimes (20 TPP and 140 TPP compute-optimal/overtrained), and a wide array of 12 downstream tasks (CoT reasoning, language understanding, safety alignment) with multiple correctness/quality metrics (Greedy, Maj@16, Pass@16, RM@16, ORM, Correct Ratio).

Addresses an important and underexplored question: whether pretraining hyperparameters selected to minimize validation loss also optimize downstream (post-trained) performance. The demonstration that higher weight decay can simultaneously worsen pretraining loss and improve downstream performance is a genuinely useful and practically relevant finding for the field.

Strong robustness checks: additional sweeps jointly varying pretraining learning rate and weight decay, and fine-tuning learning rate/weight decay/batch size, consistently show the same qualitative effect, which increases confidence in the core finding beyond a single hyperparameter configuration.

Multi-pronged mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix rank analysis building on and extending Kobayashi et al., and train-val loss gap analysis) provides plausible, converging explanations for why weight decay aids plasticity, going beyond a purely correlational headline result.

Transparent and detailed reporting: extensive appendices with hyperparameter tables, per-task figures, stability analysis of correlation coefficients (leave-one-out), and an explicit, honest limitations section that acknowledges the correlational nature of the mechanistic claims and the small sample sizes for some model groups.
weaknesses: The three proposed mechanistic explanations (linear separability, low-rank attention, reduced overfitting) are explicitly acknowledged as correlational rather than causal; no intervention experiments (e.g., directly manipulating attention rank or probing accuracy while holding weight decay fixed) are performed to disentangle these mechanisms from confounding effects of weight decay itself.

Sample sizes for the largest/most compute-intensive settings (Llama-2-4B-20x: 3 weight decay values; OLMo-2-1B-140x: 4 values) are quite small, limiting the granularity and statistical confidence of the optimal weight decay estimates in exactly the regimes (larger models, longer training) most relevant to frontier LLM practice.

All models studied (≤4B parameters, ≤210B tokens) are far smaller than modern frontier pretraining runs; the paper itself notes uncertainty about whether the optimal weight decay trend continues to decrease beyond 140 TPP, so extrapolation to very large-scale, heavily overtrained frontier models (where the practical stakes are highest) remains unverified.

The operationalized notion of "plasticity" (downstream accuracy after SFT) conflates classical plasticity (retained capacity to fit new data) with transfer/generalization quality, and it is not fully disentangled from other benefits weight decay might confer during fine-tuning itself (e.g., interacting with the FT optimizer) versus purely a property of the pretrained checkpoint.

The study only considers supervised fine-tuning as the post-training paradigm, omitting RLHF/RL-based post-training, which is increasingly central to modern LLM development pipelines and may exhibit different plasticity dynamics.

Correlation analyses between pretraining loss and downstream performance are based on small per-group sample sizes (n≤10) and are shown by the authors' own leave-one-out stability analysis (Figure 10) to be quite unstable in sign and magnitude, somewhat weakening the strength of the quantitative (though not qualitative) claims in Section 4.3.

strengths: Extensive compute investment and experimental breadth: two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple sizes (0.5B-4B), two TPP regimes (20x, 140x), and 12 downstream tasks plus a safety-alignment task, with six distinct evaluation metrics for CoT tasks.

The central framing — bridging pretraining hyperparameter choice with post-training 'plasticity' rather than only pretraining validation loss — is a useful and underexplored perspective that could influence how practitioners select pretraining hyperparameters.

Substantial robustness checks in the appendix: sweeps over pretraining learning rate jointly with weight decay (Appendix E.1) and fine-tuning learning rate/weight decay/batch size (Appendix E.2), which strengthen the claim that the qualitative effect of weight decay on downstream performance is not an artifact of one hyperparameter configuration.

Honest and specific limitations section (Appendix A) acknowledging that mechanistic explanations are correlational, that results are scope-limited, and that sample sizes are small for some model groups.

Multiple candidate mechanisms investigated (linear probing, attention-matrix rank, train-val gap) that at least offer plausible, testable explanations rather than purely post-hoc narrative, and the paper is reasonably transparent that these mechanisms conflict in some respects with prior work (e.g., Kobayashi et al. 2024's near full-rank default WD finding).
weaknesses: Statistical reliability of the key 'pretraining loss does not predict downstream performance' claim is weak: correlations are computed on very small samples (n ≤ 10, and as few as 3 for Llama-2-4B-20x), and the paper's own leave-one-out stability analysis (Figure 10) shows these correlations can flip sign and vary enormously in magnitude, undermining confidence in Finding 2 as currently quantified.

In the main experiments (Section 4.2, Figure 2), fine-tuning hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, etc.) appear to be held fixed across pretrained checkpoints with different weight decay, rather than independently tuned per checkpoint; only a small subset of this concern is addressed later (Appendix E.2) and only for 2 of 12 downstream tasks and a single model group (OLMo-2-1B-20x), leaving open the possibility that the 'optimal weight decay' conclusions are confounded by suboptimal fine-tuning hyperparameters for some checkpoints.

Scale limitations are significant relative to the claims: all pretraining runs are at most 4B parameters and at most 210B tokens, far below frontier LLM scales where weight decay's role is known to shift (as the authors themselves note, citing Bergsma et al. 2025 showing lower WD is better at high TPP). The paper's own 140 TPP OLMo-2-1B result partially contradicts the main large-WD recommendation, and it is unclear whether the 'larger than 0.1' recommendation would hold at realistic frontier scales.

The optimal weight decay values found for downstream performance (0.5–1.0) are 5–10x larger than values commonly used in practice (0.1), which is a dramatic deviation; the paper does not sufficiently interrogate whether this reflects a genuine general phenomenon or artifacts of the specific (relatively small-scale, short-horizon) training setups used.

The three mechanistic explanations in Section 5 are explicitly acknowledged by the authors to be correlational, not causal, and are not tied together into a single coherent causal story; as presented, they read more as a set of parallel observations than an explanation that predicts the quantitative pattern of plasticity gains.

The 140 TPP (overtrained) regime, which produces the most counterintuitive and headline-worthy result (higher pretraining loss but better downstream performance), is studied with only one model group and just 4 weight decay values, limiting the strength of evidence for this central 'trade-off' claim.

The term 'plasticity' is operationalized simply as fine-tuning performance after SFT, which is a reasonable but fairly narrow proxy; the connection to the richer continual-learning plasticity literature (which typically involves multiple sequential training rounds or catastrophic loss of learning capacity) is somewhat loosely drawn, bordering on relabeling 'transferability' as 'plasticity.'

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important question—whether optimizing pretraining hyperparameters for validation loss also benefits downstream fine-tuned performance—that is understudied relative to the attention given to pretraining-only scaling laws.

Very broad experimental scope: two model families (Llama-2, OLMo-2), multiple sizes (0.5B-4B), two training regimes (20 TPP and 140 TPP), 12 downstream tasks spanning CoT reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and safety alignment, and six evaluation metrics for CoT tasks.

Extensive robustness checks in the appendix (varying pretraining learning rate jointly with weight decay, and varying fine-tuning learning rate/batch size/weight decay) that consistently reproduce the core finding, strengthening confidence that the effect is not an artifact of one hyperparameter configuration.

The mechanistic investigation (linear probing for representation separability, attention matrix pseudo-rank, train-val overfitting gap) provides multiple, independently measured correlates that converge on a coherent story, and the paper explicitly and correctly flags these as correlational rather than causal explanations.

Honest and specific limitations section (small sample size for larger/overtrained model groups, scope restricted to tested models/tasks, correlational nature of mechanisms) rather than generic boilerplate.

The central causal claim (that weight decay value affects downstream performance) is well supported because weight decay is the only varied factor in matched pretraining runs, distinguishing it from the correlational mechanistic claims.
weaknesses: Some model groups (Llama-2-4B-20x: 3 weight decay values; OLMo-2-1B-140x: 4 values) have very sparse weight decay grids, making the identification of an "optimal" weight decay value for these settings weakly supported; the paper's own stability analysis (Figure 10) shows leave-one-out correlations between pretraining loss and downstream performance can flip sign, suggesting some reported relationships are fragile with small samples.

No report of run-to-run variance (e.g., multiple pretraining/fine-tuning seeds or confidence intervals) for the main results in Figures 1-3, making it hard to assess whether observed differences between adjacent weight decay values are statistically meaningful versus noise, especially given visibly non-monotonic curves in several panels (e.g., Figure 2 Greedy/Maj@16 for Llama-2-1B-20x).

All pretraining runs are at modest scale (≤4B parameters, ≤210B tokens) relative to frontier LLM training; since the paper itself shows the optimal weight decay shifts downward with increasing TPP (20x → 140x), the generalization of "higher weight decay improves plasticity" to much larger models or much higher TPP ratios used in production is speculative and explicitly flagged as uncertain by the authors.

Downstream adaptation is restricted to standard SFT; modern post-training pipelines increasingly rely on RLHF/DPO/RL-based reasoning training, and the single safety-alignment task uses a narrow setup (harmfulness reward model on 100 prompts), so claims about "post-training" more broadly are only partially substantiated.

The practical actionability of the recommendation (use weight decay > 0.1) is weakened by the fact that the optimal value varies substantially across settings (0.5, 0.6, 1.0, 0.3) without a predictive rule connecting model/data scale to the right choice, beyond the qualitative TPP-dependence trend.
